title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Priya Natarajan
body:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling guidance, the profiling playbook, the canonical benchmarking suite, release notes conventions, known issues, and operational runbooks maintained by the Serving Runtime team. It is intended for SREs, runtime engineers, platform engineers, and anyone operating or extending Redwood's inference runtime.

Scope

- Covers the Linux/GPU host level kernel scheduling patterns we recommend for GPU-backed inference nodes (NVIDIA A100/RTX/Unified APIs).
- Describes profiling methodology for latency and tail-latency investigations.
- Provides the canonical benchmarking harness and configuration format used for cost/latency trade-off analysis.
- Lists release note conventions and known issue triage steps.
- Includes operational runbooks for common incidents.

Quick summary of responsibilities

- Serving Runtime (owner): architecture, kernel scheduler integration, performance regressions, runtime-level runbooks.
- Eng-SRE: capacity planning, alerts, cluster-level mitigations.
- Eng-Infra: AMI/container base images, driver/kernel upgrades.

Architecture overview

High level: the runtime is composed of a request router, dispatcher, containerized model workers, and a shared kernel/plugin layer that implements attention kernels, continuous batching, and KV-cache management. Key components:

1) Router (redwood-router): routes requests by policy (latency SLO, cost tier, region).
2) Dispatcher (redwood-dispatch): manages batching queues, constructs micro-batches, and assigns work to workers.
3) Worker (model-worker): containerized process that runs the inference engine, exposes gRPC/HTTP endpoints for token generation.
4) Kernel plugin layer (redwood-kernels): set of custom CUDA kernels and fused operators optimized per model family.

Non-functional constraints

- P95 latency SLO: 120ms for text-generation small models (<= 7B) under steady-state.
- P99 latency SLO: 500ms for small models.
- Tail-latency budget for critical routes: 1% error budget per month.
- Cost target: keep median cost-per-token within 10% of baseline model family profile.

Kernel scheduling guidance

Goal: maximize throughput while preserving latency SLOs and minimizing preemption. Recommendations:

- GPU isolations and affinity
  - Place model-worker containers on dedicated GPUs using nvidia-docker GPU pinning (--gpus device=0). Avoid multi-tenant GPUs for latency-critical routes.
  - Use cgroup v2 CPU pinning for worker CPU threads (taskset) to isolate host scheduling variability.

- Kernel launches and stream assignment
  - Use one primary CUDA stream for inference-critical kernels and auxiliary streams for async background tasks (metrics, telemetry).
  - Ensure kernel launches are coalesced where possible; prefer fused kernels over many small kernels to reduce kernel launch overhead (see redwood-kernels/fusion-guidelines).

- Pre-emption and Cuda MPS
  - For GPUs supporting MPS, evaluate MPS for high-throughput non-latency-critical workloads. For low-latency production routes, MPS can introduce variability; default to exclusive process mode for latency-critical tooling.

- Host scheduler (Linux) tuning
  - Recommended sysctl settings (table):
  | Parameter | Recommended value | Rationale |
  |-----------|-------------------|-----------|
  | vm.swappiness | 10 | Avoid swapping model workers under memory pressure |
  | vm.dirty_ratio | 5 | Reduce dirty memory flush latency spikes |
  | sched_migration_cost_ns | 5000000 | Reduce CPU thread migrations for pinned CPU threads |

Profiling playbook (how to run a targeted investigation)

1) Reproduce at scale
   - Use the benchmark harness (see Benchmarking Suite) with the exact model version, sequence length profile, and request mix observed in production.
2) Capture traces and metrics
   - Enable distributed tracing (X-Trace) with sampling=100% for the investigation window.
   - Capture worker-side perf counters: nvprof/nsys or Nsight Systems summary (see commands).
3) Collect host level telemetry
   - top, nvidia-smi dmon, nvidia-smi pmon for process-level GPU utilization; dmesg for driver/kernel messages.

Standard commands and snippets

- Start Nsight Systems (10s warmup, 60s capture):
  sudo nsys profile --output /tmp/nsys_profile --trace=cuda,osrt -f true --duration 60s --sample=cpu

- Lightweight kernel timing (per-invocation):
  env CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 python -m runtime.bench --model resd-7b --seq 128 --batch 1 --profile --output /tmp/profile.json

- Collect perf on host (CPU scheduling):
  sudo perf record -a -g -o /tmp/perf.data sleep 60
  sudo perf report -i /tmp/perf.data

Interpreting common signals

- High kernel launch overhead: many <100us kernels with low occupancy. Fix: enable kernel fusion or increase micro-batch size.
- High CPU wait times (softirq/irq): indicates networking/driver interrupts dominating. Fix: move telemetry off critical path, increase batch sizes, shard NIC interrupts (irqbalance/affinity).
- GPU memory thrashing/ooms: frequently seen after model parameter changes or quantization mismatches. Fix: confirm quantized model binary matches runtime flags and verify CUDA memory alloc patterns.

Benchmarking suite

Purpose: reproducible latency/throughput/cost measurement across model variants and HW. The harness is stored in infra/benchmarks/serving-harness and uses a standard config format.

Canonical benchmark config (YAML-like text):
| name: resd-7b-latency-test |
| model: resd-7b:v1.12 |
| hardware: a100-80gb |
| sequence_profile: [32, 64, 128] |
| concurrency: [1, 4, 8] |
| micro_batch_size: 1 |
| duration_s: 300 |
| metrics: [p50, p95, p99, tokens_per_sec, cost_per_1k_tokens] |

Benchmark owner and acceptance criteria

- Owner: Serving Runtime Benchmarks (team lead: Marcus Lee)
- Acceptance: new kernel changes must not regress P95 by >5% for the baselines in the config matrix; any regression >5% requires a roll-forward hold and an investigation ticket.

Release notes and changelog conventions

- Release notes for runtime releases live under confluence/eng-serving-runtime/release-notes and should follow the pattern: Version, Date, Summary, Behavior changes, Performance impact, Migration steps, Rollout plan.
- Example entry:
  - Version: 2026.04.01
  - Changes: fused_attention_v2 enabled by default for resd models.
  - Impact: expected 8-12% P95 improvement for seq <= 256; potential increased GPU memory usage (+2-3%).
  - Rollout: canary 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 48 hours with rollback on >5% P95 degradation.

Known issues (top items)

1) Kernel fusion edge-case causing GPU memory leak (KERNEL-523)
   - Symptoms: GPU memory usage climbs steadily for long-lived sessions (>3h).
   - Workaround: restart model-worker every 2 hours; disable fusion via RUNTIME_FLAGS=--kernel-fusion=off for affected model families.
   - Fix status: patch in review as of 2026-04-05.

2) Sporadic P99 spikes when MPS is enabled on older drivers (DRIVER-411)
   - Symptoms: periodic 2-5s tail spikes affecting small models.
   - Workaround: disable MPS for latency-critical queues; upgrade drivers to >= 525.60.13.

3) Quantized model mismatch failure during load (QUANT-301)
   - Symptoms: model-worker OOM on load or immediate segfault during init.
   - Workaround: verify quantization profile matches build artifact; repro with the static loader tool: tools/quant-verify --model /path/to/model --profile /path/to/profile

Operational runbooks (high level)

Incident: P95 regression on production route

1) Confirm alert and scope
  - Alert triggers: p95_increase > 20% vs baseline for 10m.
  - Owner: oncall serving-runtime engineer.
2) Snapshot recent config and traces
  - Export benchmark config that matches the route. Pull distributed traces covering the window.
3) Rapid mitigation options (ordered)
  - Re-route traffic to warm fallback model variant.
  - Temporarily increase capacity on dedicated pool.
  - Disable recent runtime flag (feature flag rollback).
4) Root cause investigation
  - Run profiling playbook and open CR (change request) with artifact links.

Incident: node GPU memory OOMs causing evictions

1) Evacuate node and mark cordoned in autoscaler.
2) Collect nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.free --format=csv -l 1 for 30s.
3) Check worker logs for allocator errors (jemalloc/ptmalloc traces).
4) Rollback the last model artifact if it changed recently.

Appendix: checklist for performance-sensitive releases

1) Run canonical benchmark matrix and attach raw outputs.
2) Validate no P95 regressions >5% and P99 regressions >10% across baselines.
3) Verify Nsight/NSYS traces for kernel occupancy improvements or regressions.
4) Ship release notes with rollout plan and rollback conditions.
